item.title: Making ecological programs work at scale | Science
item.description: Some of the rain that waters the crops of farmers in Argentina and Paraguay comes from moisture released by forests in Brazil. A forest’s contribution to people’s lives can extend well beyond the land it occupies—and the carbon it stores. Forests can moderate heat, reduce soil erosion, improve air and water quality, and provide habitat for wildlife. Investing in forests need not mean choosing nature over development. Well-designed ecological programs could potentially generate ecological and health benefits that justify their costs while remaining compatible with economic growth.

item.title: Disclose trade-offs in US emissions rule change | Science
item.description: In September, the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) rolled back Biden-era greenhouse gas emissions standards for fossil fuel–fired electric generating units without quantifying the likely adverse health effects (1). A year earlier, the EPA had estimated that such a change would lead to hundreds of additional deaths annually (1, 2). The agency’s decision to exclude the evidence of harm from its deregulation of greenhouse gas emissions reverses a long-standing federal practice to provide policy-makers and the public with quantitative estimates of benefits and costs of major regulatory decisions. To ensure public accountability, US agencies should continue this long-standing tradition of promoting transparency.

item.title: Save scientific terminology from executive orders | Science
item.description: The US National Library of Medicine (NLM) maintains the controlled vocabulary used to index the global biomedical literature, and its medical subject heading of “Artificial Intelligence” has been in use since 1986 (1). However, on 29 September 2026, US President Trump ordered federal executive agencies to replace the term “artificial intelligence” with the term “super intelligence” in official documents, communications, websites, reports, and policy papers (2). Compliance with the September order is already underway: The National Institute of Standards and Technology has relabeled its evaluation research on language models and agents as super intelligence research (3). As medical researchers who depend on consistent and searchable literature, we urge US federal agencies to exempt scientific publications and controlled vocabularies from the order.
